Decide how this household would realistically spend during the current month.

Do not build an ideal budget. Do not hold spending down simply to save more.
Do not spend everything available simply because it is there. Behave like a
real Australian household with the circumstances set out below.

Anything not spent stays in savings. The total across the nine categories must
never exceed the funds available this month.

Not every category needs substantial spending every month. A realistic month
might have ordinary groceries, normal transport, recurring subscriptions and
regular pet costs, alongside no clothing purchase at all, almost no healthcare,
and then one large item: a car repair, a replaced appliance, a dental visit, a
trip away. Irregular spending should happen because it makes sense for this
household this month, not to create variety for its own sake.

Each expense belongs in exactly one category. Do not count anything twice.

Work through the categories one at a time. For each, say in one or two
sentences what this household is actually buying and reason why that amount is
right for them.

YOUR HOUSEHOLD
  An Australian household. A couple with no children at home
  Adult 1 (78): retired
  Adult 2 (83): retired
  Housing: own their home outright
  Vehicles: none, they get around by public transport and on foot

THIS MONTH (March 2022) — all amounts in Australian dollars
  Income after tax:            $0
  Government payments:         $3,060
  Housing and debt costs:      $402
  Savings:                     $73,491   (up from $59,266 a year ago)
  FUNDS AVAILABLE THIS MONTH:  $3,322

PRICES COMPARED WITH A YEAR AGO
  Alcohol and tobacco up 1.8%
  Recreation and culture up 3.0%
  Food and groceries up 4.3%
  Restaurants, cafes and takeaway up 4.3%
  Other goods and services up 5.1%
  Transport up 13.7%
  Health up 3.5%
  Clothing and footwear down 1.5%
  Furnishings and household goods up 4.9%

THE AUSTRALIAN ECONOMY THIS MONTH
  Overall inflation 5.1% over the past year · Reserve Bank cash rate 0.10% · Unemployment 4.0%

You have $3,322 available. What would a household like yours
realistically spend this month on each of the following?

  • Alcohol and tobacco — alcohol bought to drink at home from bottle shops and supermarkets, including drinks for parties, barbecues and having people over, and tobacco. Drinks bought in a pub, club or restaurant belong under restaurants
  • Recreation and culture — leisure of every kind. Streaming, music and gaming subscriptions, gym and club memberships, sport and children's activities, hobbies, books, toys and equipment, cinema, concerts, sporting events and days out, gambling, cameras, computers and audio bought for leisure, and package holidays. Any pets listed above belong here too: their food, vet bills, vaccinations, insurance, grooming and supplies. Across Australian households this is one of the largest categories of all, comparable to groceries. Subscriptions and pet costs recur; a holiday or a new computer does not
  • Food and groceries — groceries and non-alcoholic drinks for eating at home: fresh produce, meat and seafood, dairy, bread and staples, frozen food, snacks, ingredients for cooking, soft drinks. Restaurant meals, takeaway and delivery are counted separately, and pet food belongs under recreation. This is the steadiest category month to month, though it still moves with household size, prices, guests and travel
  • Restaurants, cafes and takeaway — food and drink bought away from home, and accommodation while travelling: restaurant meals, cafes, coffee out, pubs and clubs, takeaway and delivery, canteens, meals while travelling, and alcohol bought in any of those places. Also hotels, motels and other paid accommodation when away
  • Other goods and services — personal goods and services that do not sit anywhere else: haircuts, toiletries and cosmetics, childcare and school care fees, jewellery, watches and handbags, and legal, accounting or other professional services. Personal care recurs; the rest is occasional
  • Transport — the full cost of getting around, not petrol alone. Fuel or charging, servicing, repairs, tyres, batteries and parts, parking, tolls, roadside assistance, public transport, taxis and rideshare, flights and interstate fares, and buying or leasing a vehicle. Running a car costs a household far more than fuel alone once servicing, tyres, registration and repairs are counted. Fuel recurs monthly; a service, new tyres or a repair arrives occasionally and creates a spike
  • Health — healthcare paid for directly by the household: gap payments to doctors, specialists, dentists and physiotherapists, prescriptions and pharmacy, glasses and contact lenses, hospital excess. Private health insurance premiums are counted elsewhere. This varies sharply between months: often very little, then a great deal when dental work, a specialist or an illness arrives
  • Clothing and footwear — clothes and shoes for everyone in the household: everyday, work, formal and seasonal clothing, school uniforms, alterations, repairs and dry cleaning. Households often buy nothing for a month or two and then several things at once
  • Furnishings and household goods — everything used to run, maintain and equip the home. Regularly: cleaning products, laundry and dishwasher supplies, paper goods, bin bags, kitchenware, utensils, bedding and towels, light bulbs, batteries, garden supplies, tools. Occasionally: furniture, mattresses, carpets, fridges, washing machines and other whitegoods, and repairs to any of them. Also any cleaner or gardener the household pays. This is not a furniture-only category: most households spend something here every month even when they buy no furniture
